Pembrokeshire: Wales's Coastal Riding Paradise

Pembrokeshire occupies the southwestern tip of Wales, a peninsula of dramatic sea cliffs, hidden coves, and medieval towns wrapped in one of Britain's finest national parks. The riding is varied, the scenery is spectacular, and the pace is wonderfully relaxed.

The Route (100 miles)

A clockwise loop from Tenby: Tenby → Pembroke → Freshwater West → Angle → Dale → St Bride's Bay → St David's → Fishguard → Newport → return inland via the Preseli Hills.

Key Stops

  • Tenby: A walled medieval town with pastel-coloured houses overlooking golden beaches. One of the prettiest towns in Wales.
  • Pembroke Castle: Birthplace of Henry VII. Massive, imposing, and dramatically sited on a rock above the town.
  • Freshwater West: A wild, wide beach popular with surfers. The road approach gives dramatic views across the bay.
  • St David's: Britain's smallest city, home to the magnificent St David's Cathedral. The headland beyond offers dramatic clifftop walks.
  • Strumble Head: A wild headland near Fishguard with a lighthouse and views across to Ireland on clear days.

The Preseli Hills

The inland Preseli Hills — source of Stonehenge's bluestones — offer elevated moorland riding with wide views. The B4329 across the hills from Haverfordwest to Cardigan is a fine road through open, rolling landscape.

Pembrokeshire is quieter than Snowdonia and less well-known among motorcyclists. This is its great advantage — the roads are empty, the scenery rivals anywhere in Wales, and you'll have many viewpoints entirely to yourself.

Wildlife

Pembrokeshire's coast is rich in wildlife:

  • Puffins on Skomer and Skokholm islands (visible from the coast)
  • Grey seals at Martin's Haven and Ramsey Island
  • Porpoises and dolphins in Cardigan Bay
  • Choughs on the coastal cliffs

Practical Tips

  • Fuel available in all main towns. Distances are short — range is never an issue.
  • The Pembrokeshire Coast Path runs alongside many of the roads — good for short walking stops.
  • Accommodation ranges from cliff-top campsites to boutique B&Bs. Book in summer.

Planning Your Pembrokeshire Tour

Pembrokeshire is compact enough for a comfortable long weekend tour with plenty of time for exploration and relaxation. Base yourself in historic Tenby, tiny St David's, or the harbour town of Fishguard and explore the peninsula by scenic day rides. Accommodation ranges from spectacular clifftop campsites to boutique bed and breakfasts in characterful coastal towns.

Caerfai Farm campsite near St David's deserves special mention — perched on the cliffs above a stunning bay with views across to Ramsey Island. For food, the Shed at Porthgain serves fresh fish in a converted fisherman's warehouse — a unique and excellent dining experience that combines maritime heritage with outstanding seafood. The Griffin Inn in Dale is a proper sailing pub with harbour views and hearty food. Fuel is readily available in all main Pembrokeshire towns, and the distances between them are short enough that motorcycle range is never a concern on any route through this beautiful Welsh peninsula. faq.a: Pembrokeshire is quieter than Snowdonia and much less well-known among motorcyclists, which is its great advantage. The roads are empty, the coastal scenery rivals anywhere in Wales, and you will have many viewpoints entirely to yourself. It suits riders who want dramatic sea cliffs, medieval towns and relaxed touring without the tourist traffic that clogs the more famous Welsh honeypots.

faq.q: How long is the route and how long does it take?
faq.a: The suggested clockwise loop from Tenby is around 100 miles, taking in Pembroke, Freshwater West, Dale, St David's and Fishguard before returning inland over the Preseli Hills. It is compact enough for a comfortable long weekend, or a full day at a relaxed pace with stops. Pembrokeshire is small enough that motorcycle range is never a concern on any route.

Pembrokeshire's coast is rich in wildlife. Puffins nest on Skomer and Skokholm islands, visible from the coast, and grey seals haul out at Martin's Haven and Ramsey Island. Porpoises and dolphins swim in Cardigan Bay, and choughs work the coastal cliffs. Stopping at headlands such as Strumble Head and along the Pembrokeshire Coast Path gives the best chances of spotting them.

faq.q: Where should I stay and eat?
faq.a: Base yourself in historic Tenby, tiny St David's or the harbour town of Fishguard. Caerfai Farm campsite near St David's is perched on the cliffs above a stunning bay with views to Ramsey Island. For food, the Shed at Porthgain serves fresh fish in a converted fisherman's warehouse, and the Griffin Inn in Dale is a proper sailing pub with harbour views. Book ahead in summer.
